570.bp: When companies run machine learning systems in the cloud to train models on private data, users face a hard choice: trust the company to handle their data safely, or don't participate at all. This paper tackles a real bind—how can a company prove to skeptics that it's actually protecting sensitive information, without revealing its proprietary methods?
570.wh: Traditional privacy techniques add statistical noise to data (a mathematically proven safeguard), but the problem is invisible: a user has no way to know if the system actually applied the noise, or if it was silently collecting raw data instead. You must either believe the company or assume the worst.
570.ap: This work stitches together two existing tools: privacy noise (proven mathematically to block inference attacks) and cryptographic proofs (mathematical certificates anyone can verify). The system generates a proof that cryptographically attests the company did deploy the privacy mechanism correctly, without exposing the company's secret algorithms—like showing a tamper-evident seal on a package without revealing the package's contents.
570.ww: The insight is that privacy and verifiability aren't enemies; they can reinforce each other. Cryptographic proofs are short, publicly checkable, and leave no room for lying. By tethering the proof to the actual privacy mechanism, you move from blind trust to mathematical certainty.
570.po: Users can now audit that privacy was applied in outsourced machine learning, even when the system lives in untrusted cloud environments. The result is a middle ground: businesses keep their code private, but users gain verifiable proof of privacy—solving the bind.

571.bp: City governments hold meetings to debate local issues—schools, budgets, zoning—and keep formal written records. Most citizens never read these documents, partly because they're dense, verbose, and scattered across city websites. Automatic summaries could democratize access to local governance.
571.wh: Summarizing government records is harder than it sounds. A single discussion might sprawl across ten pages of back-and-forth; the system must distill it to one clear summary without losing crucial nuance or omitting dissenting views. No one had built datasets for this, especially not in Portuguese.
571.ap: This paper created a new collection: 120 actual meeting documents from Portuguese municipalities with 2,880 hand-written summaries—one summary per topic discussed. They then tested modern neural systems (both smaller tuned models and large language models) to see which could reproduce those summaries most faithfully.
571.ww: By pairing real messy documents with human-crafted gold-standard summaries, the researchers give machine learning systems something to learn from. The comparison of different summarization approaches reveals which methods actually grasp municipal records versus which merely imitate surface patterns.
571.po: Portuguese municipalities now have a benchmark to build better summarization tools, making it cheaper and faster to create readable summaries of civic meetings. Citizens in a non-English-speaking region can finally access what their government decided without reading thirty pages.

572.bp: Generative AI can now create convincing fake videos of people saying things they never said. Security cameras, body-cam footage, and any video evidence could be forged, threatening police investigations, insurance claims, and courtroom testimony. We need a way to prove that recorded footage hasn't been tampered with.
572.wh: Full end-to-end provenance—tracking footage from the camera's sensor all the way through storage—requires tight control of every device in a chain. In practice, security cameras are old, diverse, and scattered; you can't retrofit cryptographic signing into every one. You need a simpler solution that still catches tampering after the fact.
572.ap: This system uses blockchain (a tamper-evident ledger) to timestamp and log video segments, and then stores the actual video on a decentralized network (IPFS). When someone claims a video is authentic, you can check the blockchain to see whether the video's fingerprint was logged at the claimed date and time.
572.ww: Blockchain acts as a notary—it doesn't guarantee the video is real, but it does create an immutable record of 'this video's fingerprint was registered on this date,' making it provably impossible to swap in a forged video retroactively. The decentralized storage ensures no single actor can erase the evidence.
572.po: Security systems can now register footage in real-time with a cost of about 57 cents per recording—expensive for casual use, but viable for high-value evidence like crime scenes. An investigator can prove that a video existed unchanged on a specific date, blocking the 'it was edited later' defense.

573.bp: When you buy online, your behavior tells a story: you browse an item, add it to your cart, maybe abandon it, then later purchase. Recommendation systems need to predict your next action, but they also need to explain why they made that recommendation—users don't trust opaque machine answers.
573.wh: User behavior chains have hidden confounders: maybe you looked at winter coats because friends were talking about skiing, not because you plan to buy. A naive system sees the browse-cart-buy pattern and learns it as a rule, but that rule could be wrong if you only bought because of a price drop unrelated to browsing. Explainability makes this worse: most methods that explain predictions require outside data (product metadata, user profiles), which isn't always available.
573.ap: This work models behavior as a chain of logical decisions, where each step (view → cart → buy) is governed by hidden rules that can be expressed in plain logic (AND, OR operations). It separates the true causal path from spurious patterns caused by confounders, then uses those causal paths to explain predictions in human-readable logic: 'System predicted buy because: user viewed the item AND user added to cart.'
573.ww: Human decisions follow rules we can articulate; the system mirrors this by backing up each prediction with explicit logical statements that can be checked. By removing the effect of confounders first, the logic it finds is more trustworthy than a pattern learned from raw data.
573.po: Recommendation systems can now output explanations that customers understand and can argue with, while the underlying causal reasoning means recommendations are more faithful to true preferences rather than spurious correlations. Businesses get both better accuracy and better explainability.

574.bp: Machine translation and text analysis work well for major languages like English and Mandarin, but for smaller languages—especially those with limited online text—these systems perform poorly. Yet billions of people speak low-resource languages and need these tools. How do you scale sophisticated AI analysis to languages with scarce training data?
574.wh: The field is split into two camps: one focuses on engineering (scaling compute and data pipelines) while the other focuses on model tweaks (injecting linguistic knowledge into the model itself). Each solves half the problem, but neither alone bridges the gap between what works for big languages and what works for long-tail languages.
574.ap: This paper fuses both camps by building a three-stage pipeline: first, enhance training by injecting linguistic structure (like grammar rules); second, use a feedback loop during learning to diagnose errors in specific cases and adjust the training plan; third, at inference time, use a smarter decoding algorithm that samples candidate outputs and picks the one least likely to confuse or mislead. All three stages reinforce each other.
574.ww: Linguistic structure gives the model a skeleton to build on (it learns faster and more robustly), error feedback tells the system where it's going wrong so it can focus effort, and smart decoding guards against hallucinations. Together they handle the messiness of low-resource data that would confound a simpler approach.
574.po: Translation and analysis of low-resource languages improved by over 2 points on a standard benchmark—a significant jump. Critically, the system now scales to web-size content in underserved languages, making real-world AI tools accessible to non-English speakers.

575.bp: Large language models now power web search: you ask a question, the system retrieves relevant documents, and the model writes an answer. But the model's attention mechanism (which decides which parts of the retrieved documents to focus on) becomes crushingly slow when there are thousands of pages of content, making real-time answers impossible.
575.wh: An ideal solution would predict in advance which parts of the documents the model will need and skip the rest. But predicting before you've actually run inference creates a chicken-and-egg problem: you need to know the answer to know what to skip, but you're running inference to find the answer.
575.ap: This paper exploits a trick already used in web search: speculative decoding (a lightweight model guesses the answer first, fast). While that lightweight model is running, this system also scans the document to predict which parts matter most, then fetches only those parts when the main model needs them. It's like the lightweight model serves double duty: generating candidate answers and mapping the document.
575.ww: Speculative decoding is already free in production, so piggybacking the scanning step onto it costs nothing. By predicting salient content dynamically based on what's actually in the documents, the system adapts to diverse web content (multilingual, multi-topic) in a way fixed pruning never could.
575.po: Web-scale search now processes long, diverse document collections faster, since the model only loads the parts it needs into memory. This makes real-time AI-powered search economically viable for companies running at massive scale.

576.bp: Planning a trip requires balancing flights, hotels, preferences, and budget while managing information overload. Web interfaces still treat all users the same, showing the same menus and pacing, even though some users are tired and struggling to think straight while others are focused and quick. A smarter interface would adapt to the user's mental state in real-time.
576.wh: Interfaces can't read minds, so they don't know when a user is overwhelmed or losing focus. Traditional solutions either slow everything down (helping tired users but frustrating sharp ones) or speed up (overwhelming fatigued users). You'd need to measure the user's attention and emotional state moment-to-moment, which no current system does.
576.ap: This system watches the user's face (detecting facial expressions) and eyes (tracking where they're looking and how stable they are) to infer mental state. A set of intelligent agents then coordinate their help: some handle complex reasoning, others explain, others pace feedback. The system adjusts reasoning depth and feedback timing based on detected emotional and attentional state.
576.ww: Facial and gaze signals are mirrors of cognition: if your eyes are darting and your face shows stress, you're overloaded; if you're calm and focused, you can handle complexity. By matching interface support to these signals, the system meets users where they are rather than forcing them to adapt.
576.po: Users who got adaptive support made better decisions and used less mental effort than those with fixed interfaces. This represents a concrete 10% improvement in decision quality with no increase in cognitive cost—proof that real-time adaptation based on user state works.

577.bp: Doxing—publishing someone's private information online—was once sporadic vigilantism. In Chinese online spaces, it has evolved into an industrialized market where companies offer personal data as a product. This threatens millions of people's privacy and safety. Understanding how this market operates is the first step to stopping it.
577.wh: Underground data markets are hidden by design. Researchers can't simply ask participants where they operate or how they work. Studying the ecosystem requires finding where it's actually visible and analyzing patterns at scale—a data forensics challenge.
577.ap: The researchers analyzed millions of messages and links from a major Chinese messaging platform where doxing services advertise. They mapped out the supply chain (data sources → service providers → buyers), counted how many people used these services, tracked payment methods, and documented the six main service categories offered.
577.ww: Mass analysis reveals structure: by looking at patterns across thousands of transactions, the researchers could infer roles (who supplies data, who resells it, who buys it), organization (the three-tier chain), and sustainability mechanisms (advertising, payment systems). Individual messages hide what aggregate patterns expose.
577.po: The study documents a mature, hardened market worth millions annually, revealing exactly where regulation and law enforcement should focus. The data also shows which platforms inadvertently harbor these services, enabling targeted interventions.

578.bp: Companies deploy guardrails (safety filters) around language models to block harmful requests. Users shouldn't be able to jailbreak the model by asking questions in clever ways. But guardrails and the core model see language differently—what looks garbled to the filter might be clear to the model, creating a security gap.
578.wh: Guardrails typically scan input text character-by-character for suspicious patterns, and models process language semantically (grasping meaning regardless of typos). An adversary could exploit this mismatch: add garbage characters that fool the filter but leave meaning intact for the model.
578.ap: This paper demonstrates the gap by perturbing input text (adding misspellings, Unicode tricks) and then 'coaching' the model to recover the original intent via chain-of-thought prompting. This two-step attack—noise plus guidance—bypasses state-of-the-art guardrails while remaining interpretable to the model.
578.ww: The asymmetry exists because guardrails prioritize speed (simple text scanning) while models prioritize understanding (deep semantic processing). You can't just patch one without redesigning both, because the mismatch is architectural, not accidental.
578.po: The findings expose critical flaws in current defenses and identify a 'success interval' where perturbations evade detection yet preserve meaning—establishing that guardrails and models need to be co-designed, not bolted together.

579.bp: Designing new drugs requires finding molecules that bind tightly to disease-causing proteins. This is normally done by chemists testing thousands of candidates in the lab. Language models can generate candidate molecules digitally, but they often produce chemically impossible or synthesizable dead-ends. How do you make language models actually useful for drug design?
579.wh: Language models don't deeply understand 3D protein structure or chemical feasibility—they're trained on language, not molecules. If you just ask a model to generate a molecule, it often hallucinates something that looks right on paper but would fall apart in reality or be impossible to make.
579.ap: This work reframes the problem: treat the model's generation as a two-part process: (1) explore the space of possible molecules by searching through the model's learned representations, testing candidates against protein binding, and (2) decode only the parts the model knows well, letting simpler rules handle the risky parts. A Bayesian optimizer systematically searches for promising candidates during exploration.
579.ww: This mirrors how chemists actually work: they explore (trying different molecular families based on binding science) and then locally optimize (tweaking a promising lead compound). By explicitly separating exploration from familiar territory, the system avoids the model inventing nonsense in unfamiliar regions of molecular space.
579.po: Language models can now generate drug candidates with high binding affinity to target proteins, outperforming simpler baselines. The system makes models useful for early-stage drug discovery, where fast generation and screening matter more than perfection.

580.bp: Cities want to coordinate drone fleets for delivery to serve many locations efficiently. Each drone makes its own local decisions (where to fly, whom to serve), but collective behavior emerges from millions of individual choices. Can physics and statistical mechanics offer insight into how to coordinate them?
580.wh: Centralized control of thousands of drones would be computationally intractable. Decentralized coordination means drones make selfish local decisions, which can cascade into chaos (all drones racing to the same popular location, leaving others empty). You need a principled way to balance exploration and exploitation across the fleet.
580.ap: This paper borrows ideas from thermodynamics: each drone has an energy function that represents its preferences (travel cost, service fairness, avoiding other drones), and it makes probabilistic choices following a 'Gibbs policy'—a statistical principle from physics. Adjusting a temperature parameter T shifts the whole fleet between rigid coordination and exploration.
580.ww: Physics already solved analogous problems: systems of particles follow simple local rules and produce coherent large-scale behavior. By encoding drone objectives as energy functions and applying statistical mechanics, the system's emergent behavior becomes predictable and tunable.
580.po: The phase diagram reveals precisely how fleet behavior changes with parameters—highly coordinated at low T, chaotic at intermediate T, partially recovering at high T. This gives city planners a tool to dial in desired behavior without redesigning the control algorithm.

581.bp: Scientific papers make specific claims ('compound X binds to protein Y'). Fact-checking these claims against the scientific literature is vital for detecting fraud and misinformation, but is hard because technical claims require careful verification in domain-specific sources, and those sources may not be immediately available.
581.wh: A naive fact-checker might hallucinate false evidence or apply reasoning inconsistently. With thousands of claims to check and limited time (and cost), you can't look up every single one—you'd need to decide which claims need verification from external sources and which can be trusted based on provided context.
581.ap: This system breaks claims into atomic facts, aligns each to context snippets, and runs a calibrated checker to gauge confidence. If confidence is low (uncertain), it triggers a limited web search over authoritative sources. Critically, it avoids overriding provided context with web evidence when they disagree; instead, it abstains from a judgment.
581.ww: Atomic decomposition lets the system reason about parts rather than wholes, reducing hallucination risk. Calibration—knowing when you don't know—enables smart triage: web searches happen rarely, conserving cost and time, while still catching false claims.
581.po: Scientific fact-checking now exceeds baseline performance while using external evidence selectively. Researchers can detect unsupported claims in papers faster and more reliably, reducing the effort needed to vet scientific work.

582.bp: Cryptocurrencies live on blockchains and are traded on two kinds of markets: centralized exchanges (CEX, run by companies) and decentralized exchanges (DEX, run by smart contracts). Prices across the two sometimes diverge, creating free money for arbitrageurs who buy low on one and sell high on the other.
582.wh: Prices fluctuate randomly and chaotically; simple models miss the structure. You need to account for market microstructure (how prices evolve stochastically) and fit models to actual blockchain data to predict when and where arbitrage opportunities will emerge.
582.ap: This paper applies Hidden Markov Models—a statistical tool from finance—to cryptocurrency price movements. They extract transaction logs from the Ethereum blockchain, fit HMM parameters to observed price paths, and use the learned model to forecast when prices will diverge between CEX and DEX.
582.ww: Hidden Markov Models excel at capturing regime changes: prices might behave one way during high volatility and differently during calm markets. By learning these regimes from data, the system can anticipate regime transitions and predict where arbitrage opportunities emerge.
582.po: Arbitrage bots can now predict CEX-DEX price divergences more accurately, allowing faster trades and capturing more profit. The model also reveals DeFi market characteristics, helping researchers understand how prices evolve in decentralized finance.

583.bp: Hateful memes combine innocent-looking images and text in ways that convey bigotry—the harm emerges from the interaction, not from either part alone. Detecting these requires understanding both image and text and their interplay. Do modern thinking-capable language models succeed at this nuanced task?
583.wh: Most off-the-shelf vision-language models aren't trained on hateful memes, so they perform poorly. You could retrain them, but that requires high-quality step-by-step explanations (chain-of-thought rationales) that don't exist in large quantities.
583.ap: The researchers extended the dataset by generating weak explanations via distillation (having better models generate rough drafts), then fine-tuned a thinking model with a new reinforcement learning objective that rewards both correct classification and high-quality explanations. The objective balances classification and reasoning quality.
583.ww: Weak supervision lets you grow training data beyond manual annotations, and reinforcement learning lets you reward intermediate reasoning—the steps matter, not just the answer. By forcing the model to show its work and rewarding explanations, the system learns finer-grained reasoning than classification alone.
583.po: The model now detects hateful memes more accurately and generates clearer explanations for its decisions. This is a step toward trustworthy content moderation: humans can audit why the system flagged something, not just accept a yes-or-no verdict.

584.bp: Agentic AI—systems that autonomously plan and execute tasks—is a hot topic today. But the vision of autonomous agents living on the semantic web and coordinating via formally defined services predates large language models by decades. What can today's AI learn from those older ideas?
584.wh: Agentic AI research is proceeding without strong historical grounding. Researchers invent new abstractions for agent coordination, planning, and service composition, unaware that the Semantic Web and Web Services communities solved similar problems twenty years ago.
584.ap: This short talk draws parallels: Semantic Web concepts (ontologies that formally describe entities and services, reasoning over these descriptions, service composition) map cleanly onto agentic AI. The paper argues that classical approaches to service definition, discovery, and orchestration apply directly to modern agents.
584.ww: Older work had incomplete solutions but correct intuitions: the need for formal specifications, composability, and decentralized coordination are just as relevant for today's agents as they were for web services. Reusing these ideas saves reinvention and brings solutions to known hard problems.
584.po: The result is a conceptual bridge: researchers designing agentic AI can draw on decades of Web Services scholarship. This doesn't solve all new challenges (LLMs add unpredictability older systems didn't face), but it focuses research on genuinely new problems rather than rehashing solved ones.
